execution.build: one `package main` in that one file, compiled from that file alone with the toolchain installed here, so a helper split into a sibling source beside it never reaches the build however that sibling declares itself
execution.dependencies: the Go standard library and nothing beyond it
execution.process: a run does its work itself and starts no other process: not through os/exec or plugin, not through os.StartProcess or syscall.Exec/ForkExec/StartProcess, and not by handing a process-creating number such as SYS_EXECVE, SYS_FORK, SYS_VFORK or SYS_CLONE to a raw syscall. Ordinary system calls through the same entry point -- an fsync on a file the run itself wrote, say -- are the run's own work and are not restricted
execution.side_effects: when a run finishes, nothing outside the directory it wrote into has been added to, changed or taken away by it; scratch elsewhere is the run's own business while it lasts and goes when the run does

cli.input: --input selects the resolved rule base only; default /app/data/policy_rules.json
cli.output_dir_handling: the run clears what an earlier run left in the output directory and writes its own three files there; the directory itself is not removed and recreated, since the run does not own the path it writes into

description: Output contract for the firewall policy compiler. Shapes, paths, field lists and sort orders only; no derivation rule lives here.

field_notes.default_row: the closing deny the run appends is never shadowed and names no shadower: it carries `shadowed` false and `shadowed_by` the empty string, whatever the rules above it do

field_types.shadowed_by: string, the empty string where the rule is not shadowed

compiled_policy.serialisation: JSON array, two-space indent, trailing newline

exception_queue.serialisation: one compact JSON object per line, trailing newline

field_notes.compiled_count: the rows the compiled policy carries, the closing deny among them
field_notes.deny_count: the rows of the COMPILED POLICY whose action is deny, the closing deny among them: like permit_count it counts what the policy carries rather than what the base offered, so a deny that was set aside as inert or queued over the cap is not among them
field_notes.permit_count: the rows of the COMPILED POLICY whose action is permit, counted the same way, so permit_count and deny_count together come to compiled_count
field_notes.enabled_rule_count: the rules the rebuilt base carries with `enabled` true, counted as read and before any of them is set aside: a rule enabled but inert is counted here and by inert_count both
field_notes.queued_count: the rows the exception queue carries
field_notes.rule_count: the rules the base handed to --input carries, counted as read

summary.serialisation: JSON object, two-space indent, trailing newline

constraints: every sequence is a non-negative integer strictly below the policy's default_deny_sequence, so the closing deny is always the last row of the compiled policy and the contract's ascending sort holds over the whole array
FW-DEFAULT is reserved for the closing deny and is never an operator rule id
rule ids are unique within a rule base

field_notes.sequence: the operator's own ordering, ascending and strictly below default_deny_sequence; the device takes the first matching rule in it

policy_rules.serialisation: JSON array, two-space indent, trailing newline

object_groups.note: resolved during the rule-base rebuild, not re-read at compile time

runtime_budget_note: guidance on the scale a run is expected to handle, not a graded ceiling: the verifier bounds its own run rather than timing this one

units.address_span: a count of IPv4 addresses read off the rule's source set; how a set whose prefixes overlap is counted is a governance decision and is not settled here
units.cidr: dotted-quad IPv4 prefix with a length, network address already masked
